analysis.one_liner: Strips tax breaks from major oil companies, recovers Gulf royalties, and bans gas price gouging in emergencies.
analysis.headline: A Democratic bill targeting big oil's tax breaks and Gulf royalty relief gathered 19 cosponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended in January 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have taken three main steps against high gas prices in 2011: it would have ended three special tax deductions that only the biggest, fully integrated oil companies enjoy; it would have forced companies holding older Gulf of Mexico leases to renegotiate leases that let them skip royalty payments when oil prices are high; and it would have made it illegal for sellers to charge unconscionably excessive gasoline prices during an internationally proclaimed oil-market crisis, with fines of up to three times the profits gained or $100 million, plus criminal fines up to $500 million for repeat violators. It also would have let the Energy Department sell up to 30 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve and use the proceeds to buy refined fuel for the reserve, and would have directed all Gulf royalty money to deficit and debt reduction.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who buy gasoline, and federal taxpayers. The tax provisions would have directed revenue from the largest oil companies toward deficit and debt reduction, and the royalty provisions would have recovered public money from Gulf leases issued in the late 1990s that let companies drill royalty-free unless prices exceeded set thresholds. The price gouging ban would have protected drivers during emergencies, and the Strategic Petroleum Reserve provisions gave the President a new tool against market manipulation.

how_it_helps.text: Ends the domestic production tax deduction, last-in first-out inventory accounting, and the intangible drilling cost deduction for major integrated oil companies, and requires that all Gulf royalty and rental money be deposited in the Treasury for deficit or debt reduction [S2] [S3].

Bars new Gulf of Mexico leases and lease transfers to holders of covered royalty-relief leases unless they renegotiate to pay royalties when prices meet statutory thresholds, and requires the Interior Secretary to grant lessee requests to add such price thresholds to leases issued between 1996 and 2000 [S2] [S3].

Makes unconscionably excessive gasoline pricing during a proclaimed international oil-market crisis unlawful, enforced by the FTC with priority for companies over $10 billion in annual fuel sales, with civil penalties up to triple the violator's profits or $100 million, criminal fines up to $500 million, and enforcement rights for state attorneys general [S2] [S3].

Authorizes the sale of up to 30 million barrels from the Strategic Petroleum Reserve with proceeds used to acquire refined product, and creates a presidential authority to draw down up to 30 million barrels to address market manipulation or otherwise serve the public interest [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: The major integrated oil companies — the handful of firms that both produce and refine oil — which would have lost three tax deductions, and Gulf of Mexico leaseholders holding pre-2001 royalty-relief leases, which would have faced renegotiated royalty payments. Wholesalers and retailers could also face penalties for price gouging during declared emergencies. Some portion of the oil companies' added costs could ultimately be reflected in fuel prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill's Strategic Petroleum Reserve release is limited to 30 million barrels, a small fraction of annual U.S. consumption, so its direct effect on pump prices would likely have been modest [S3].

Removing the deductions raises the biggest oil companies' costs, and economists generally expect some of such cost increases to be passed through to consumers in fuel prices, so the consumer benefit of the tax title is indirect.

A federal price-gouging standard triggered by presidential proclamation could discourage wholesalers from rushing extra fuel into a crisis area if selling above prior prices risks penalties, a tradeoff critics of such laws commonly raise.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The strongest provision was the royalty title, which targets leases issued in 1996-2000 that allowed royalty relief at price thresholds well below the prices of 2011 — an approach even the bill itself invited lessees to accept voluntarily. The tax title raised real money but only from the largest integrated firms, with some pass-through risk to consumers, and the gouging ban and reserve release were narrower tools whose price effects would likely have been modest. On balance the bill's benefits to taxpayers and drivers outweighed its costs, though it was not designed to dramatically lower pump prices on its own.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced and then to two subcommittees, and it sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote until the Congress ended in January 2013.

narrative.text: Rep. Tim Bishop of New York introduced the bill on May 5, 2011, joined by Reps. Edward Markey, Judy Chu, and John Larson [S1] [S3] [S5].

The same day, the Speaker referred it to the Committees on Energy and Commerce, Ways and Means, and Natural Resources; within two weeks it went to the Commerce, Manufacturing, and Trade Subcommittee and the Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee [S5].
It drew 19 additional cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and no further action of any kind followed [S4] [S5].
The bill never received a committee hearing or markup, never reached the House floor, and died when the 112th Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Major integrated oil companies came out ahead: they kept the three tax deductions the bill would have repealed, and holders of pre-2001 Gulf royalty-relief leases kept drilling without renegotiated royalty payments. House Republicans were spared a recorded vote on oil-industry tax provisions.

for.name: Rep. Tim Bishop

for.name: Nancy Pelosi
for.what_they_did: Backed oil-company tax-break repeal legislation during the 2011 gas price spike.

against.role: Controlled the House floor calendar and committee scheduling in the 112th Congress

against.name: American Petroleum Institute and the major oil companies
against.role: Oil and gas industry trade association and largest integrated producers
against.what_they_did: Fought proposals in 2011 to repeal oil-industry tax deductions, arguing they would raise energy costs and discourage domestic production.

sides.party_line_note: All 20 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-majority House never acted on the bill.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their domestic production deduction, LIFO inventory accounting, and intangible drilling cost deductions — tax benefits worth billions to the largest firms — and subjected them to priority enforcement of the price gouging ban. Their interest in keeping these deductions ran against taxpayers who fund deficit reduction with them in place.

industries.industry: Gulf of Mexico oil and gas lessees with royalty-relief leases
industries.note: Holders of pre-2001 deepwater leases that suspend royalties until prices cross old, low thresholds would have had to renegotiate to pay royalties at higher price thresholds, or lose eligibility for new leases and lease transfers. Every dollar of renegotiated royalty is public revenue that now stays with the leaseholder.

They would have faced new federal penalties — up to triple illicit profits or $100 million in civil fines, plus criminal fines up to $500 million — for unconscionable pricing during declared oil-market emergencies, but only during such proclamations, and enforcement priority targeted companies with over $10 billion in annual fuel sales rather than small stations.
